THOUGHT: The patient is a 69-year-old male with a clear, persistent pattern of falling asleep very early in the evening (unable to stay awake past 6 pm) and waking up early, yet feeling fully rested upon awakening. This is not insomnia (which would involve difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep *despite opportunity* and typically includes nonrestorative sleep), nor is it hypersomnia (since he is alert and refreshed after sleep). His social functioning is impaired—specifically, his ability to participate in shared evening activities with his wife—indicating a misalignment between his endogenous circadian rhythm and societal/relationship demands. The timing of symptoms (early sleep onset/wake time), age (advanced sleep phase disorder [ASPD] is common in older adults), retirement (removal of external time cues like work schedules), and lack of response to caffeine (a stimulant that does not reset circadian phase) all support a circadian etiology. Crucially, objective testing confirms the diagnosis: polysomnography shows normal sleep efficiency but advanced sleep phase, and melatonin levels peak abnormally early in the evening—consistent with a phase-advanced circadian pacemaker. Actigraphy further corroborates stable, early sleep-wake timing over two weeks. No evidence of other sleep disorders (e.g., sleep apnea, periodic limb movements) or neurological deficits on exam. IBS is unrelated and well-controlled. Thus, all clinical and objective data converge on Advanced Sleep-Wake Phase Disorder (ASPD), formerly known as Advanced Sleep Phase Syndrome (ASPS).

DIAGNOSIS: Advanced Sleep-Wake Phase Disorder
